thread.title: Netflix: Why It Won't Rally - Netflix, Inc. (NASDAQ:NFLX) | Seeking Alpha

author: Michael Wiggins De Oliveira
title: Netflix: Why It Won't Rally - Netflix, Inc. (NASDAQ:NFLX) | Seeking Alpha
text:
Investment Thesis Netflix ( NFLX ) is an investment I have been bearish on for some time. Furthermore, while there have been plenty of opportunities to jump to the sidelines, it is still not too late. For now, Netflix remains too risky an investment.
Recent Developments 2018 turned out to be a great year for value investors. While I'll be the first to admit that my portfolio has struggled during 2018, I can objectively and realistically look at my portfolio and see just how cheap all my investments are. In fact, I have little doubts that most of my positions will see better days over the near and medium term. But I cannot say the same about Netflix.
Further, while Netflix often gets grouped together as a FAANG stock, I believe this is incorrect. Netflix's problems are in a league of their own. For example, one can not seriously argue that Apple ( AAPL ) with its rock solid balance sheet and strong competitive advantage is in any shape, form or valuation related to Netflix. Apple too will see better days. Once again, it is my strong contention that Netflix will not.
Upcoming trouble - Do Not Ignore Most readers are highly dismissive of Netflix's consistent debt raises. However, I affirm: ignore the debt raises at your peril. In fact, I insist that the most recent debt raises are a telling sign of upcoming trouble.
Here are the two recent debt raises:
€1.1 billion (roughly $1.25 billion) aggregate principal amount at 4.625% Senior Notes due 2029. $800 million aggregate principal amount at 6.375% Senior Notes due 2029. Now, if we look over the table below, highlighted in blue is Netflix's previous euro-denominated debt raise (converted to U.S. dollars)
And we can clearly see that Netflix's recent debt raise carries a 1% higher interest, which implies that debt markets are now asking for higher yields as interest rates are starting to rise. Additionally, we can see that Netflix's U.S. dollar-denominated notes also carry a higher, more enticing yield than Netflix has ever before had to offer.
Said another way, so far, Netflix's interest expense has hovered around 3% of revenues. However, given these most recent debt raises carry higher coupons, shareholders should be expecting Netflix's interest expense to gravitate towards 4% of revenue.
Now going forward, including these recent raises, Netflix has roughly $5 billion of cash and equivalents on its balance sheet during Q4 2018. However, at the same time, Netflix's has guided that Q4 FCF deficit will increase sequentially from Q3 to Q4, causing a cash burn of around $1.3 billion. In summary, in the best case scenario, Netflix's cash and equivalents finish Q4 2018 with around $3.8 billion.
"A banker is a fellow who lends you his umbrella when the sun is shining, but wants it back the minute it begins to rain."
- Mark Twain
Looking forward, we know that Netflix has already guided for FY 2019 free cash flow burn of $3 billion - which means that Netflix will very soon, around March 2019, need to once again resort to debt markets to raise capital . However, the problem for Netflix will be the fact that debt markets only like to lend you capital when it's sunny. But when confidence erodes, it can be extraordinarily difficult to raise capital. And as we have clearly seen over the past several months, with Netflix's shares selling off more than 35% from its highs, investors are finally starting to question Netflix's business model and confidence in Netflix is being brought into question.
Content Is Great - So Everyone Is Doing It I have been arguing elsewhere on SA that 2019 will be a great year for content. Every company with strong financial resources has latched on to the idea that content increases the stickiness of their respective platforms.
In the U.S., we have Amazon Video ( AMZN ), Apple ( AAPL ), Facebook Watch ( FB ), Alphabet's ( GOOGL ) (NASDAQ: GOOG ) YouTube, Walmart's VUDU ( WMT ) to name a few, while on the other side of the world, Alibaba ( BABA ) has Youko with daily average subscribers increasing 100% YoY. All in all, 2019 will be fantastic for viewers.
The problem for Netflix will be, how to retain key talent? Producing top-rated scripted content will become prohibitively expensive. Because decent scriptwriters will simply be able to auction-off their best content to the highest bidder.
Moreover, on the other side of the equation, with so much top-rated content available at a whole range of price points, Netflix's budget-priced content package, its key competitive advantage , will dwindle - as many well-funded peers, such as Apple and Amazon, are likely to continue to offer their content to consumers for free (or nearly free). While other consumers, with deeper pockets, may opt to go for Disney+ ( DIS ) or something altogether different.
Valuation As an investor, although the above discussion makes for an interesting dynamic going into 2019, what matters at the end of the day is less about who will win the content war, and more about how shareholders will fare.
Source: author's calculations, morningstar.com
The above table leads one to believe that Netflix is not likely to be a winning investment in 2019. Now, that may seem at odds with what many shareholders may be expecting. In fact, I suspect that many shareholders will think that Netflix's recent sell-off is only temporary. I, on the other hand, strongly contend that it is not temporary.
As the table shows, amongst its peers, such as Alphabet (owner of YouTube), Disney and Discovery ( DISCK ), Netflix is the only company which is consistently unable to generate cash flows from operations. In fact, any reasonable mind can look at the above table and pick out, by far and wide, that Netflix is the most expensively priced peer in the table.
Takeaway In the above article, I argue that Netflix's recent sell-off is not temporary. That its share price will not be returning to former glory any time soon. And that, if anything, 2019 is set up to be an even more challenging year for Netflix, but that many investors are not accurately pricing in these prospects.
Disclaimer: Please do your own due diligence to reach your own conclusions.
